column2: This is the path of the yogas, by which they go to that state; the steadfast, having conquered fatigue by their posture, set the self in the head.
Thus it is ordained in the prana and apana of all embodied beings; fire stays in it always, collected as in a pot.
[Bharadvaja said:] "If heat is of fire's nature and is cooked by fire, and if fire digests, then the soul is useless.
When a creature dies, the soul is not found; the wind alone leaves him and the heat perishes.
If the soul is like wind, joined with the wind, it would be seen like a circle of wind and go with the hosts of Maruts.
If it is joined with wind and perishes from it, then, like water in a vessel freed in a great ocean, it would be another thing.
As water poured into a well, or a lamp cast into fire, quickly perishes, so does this.
In this body common to five, where is life? When any one of four of them is abandoned, there is no holding together.
Water perishes from lack of food; wind from the checking of breath; space perishes from the splitting of the belly; fire perishes from not eating.
By disease, wounds and distress the earth also crumbles; when any one of these is afflicted the compound goes fivefold apart.
This cow will carry me across to the other world: the creature who dies after giving, whom will that cow carry across?
When the cow, the receiver and the giver all alike dissolve right here, where can there be a meeting for them?
For one eaten by birds, or fallen from a mountain peak, or consumed by fire, where is revival again?
If a tree is cut and the root does not sprout, but its seeds go on, where would the dead one return?
Only the seed was created before, and this goes on turning; the dead die and perish, and seed from seed goes on."
[Bhrigu said:] "The soul does not rest on the body and perish when it perishes, as fire does not perish when the fuel is burnt."
[Bharadvaja said:] "If there were no destruction of fire in that way, at the end of the use of the fuel that fire would not be found.
I know it only as perishing, the fire become quiet without fuel, whose course, measure or form is not seen."
[Bhrigu said:] "At the end of the use of fuel, the fire, though it is there, is not seen; it is hard to grasp, following space, and without a support.
So at the leaving of the body the soul stays like space; it is not grasped because of its great subtlety, like light, without doubt.
Fire holds the breaths; let that be understood as the soul; fire sustained by wind perishes by the checking of breath.
When that fire of the body has perished, the body is insensible; it falls and goes to the state of earth, for the earth is its resort.
For all the moving and the unmoving, wind goes to space, and light follows it; there the three are one, and two are established on earth."
[Bharadvaja said:] "When the body is split, in the mass of flesh and blood, the heap of fat, sinew and bone, the soul is not found.
If the body is lifeless, joined with the five elements, who feels that pain in sorrow of body and mind?
The soul hears what is said with the ears; but great sage, when the mind is distracted it does not hear; therefore the soul is useless.
One sees all that is to be seen with the eye joined to the mind; when the mind is troubled, one, though looking, does not see.
One who is under the sway of sleep does not see, speak, hear or smell, and does not know touch or taste.
Who rejoices, who is angry, who grieves, who is alarmed? Who wishes, who meditates, who hates, who utters speech?"
[Bhrigu said:] "Nothing here is common to five; the inner self alone bears the body. He knows smells, tastes, sound, touch and form, and the other qualities.
In the five-element body, the displayer of the five qualities, the inner self, following all the limbs, knows the sorrows and pleasures here; through separation from it the body knows nothing.
When there is no form, no touch, and no heat of fire, then, when the fire of the body is stilled, he leaves the body and it perishes.
All this is made of water; water is the form of the embodied; in it the self, the mental Brahma, is the maker of the worlds in all beings.
Know that self, whose nature is the good of all the worlds, resting in that body like a drop of water on a lotus.
Know him as the knower of the field, ever of the nature of the world's good; know tamas, rajas and sattva as these qualities of the soul.
They say that the soul's quality is consciousness; he moves and moves all; and beyond that they call the knower of the field, who sets in motion the seven worlds.

There is no destruction of the soul when the body breaks; the unawake call this false, saying 'he is dead'; the soul goes on, separated from the body; the breaking of the body is only its half of ten.
So he moves hidden and covered in all beings; but he is seen by the supreme, subtle intellect of those who see the truth.
The wise man, ever joined to him in the early and late hours of the night, light in diet and pure of self, sees the self in the self.
By the clearing of the mind, putting aside deeds good and bad, with serene self, abiding in the self, he enjoys imperishable happiness.
The mental fire in bodies is called the soul; this is the creation of Prajapati in the determination of the elements and the self."
[Bhrigu said:] "Then the lord ordained truth, dharma, austerity, the eternal Brahman, conduct and purity for heaven.
Gods, Danavas, gandharvas, Daityas, asuras, great serpents, yakshas, rakshasas, nagas, pishachas and men,
brahmanas, kshatriyas, vaishyas and shudras, best of the twice-born, and the other hosts of beings, he made also.
The colour of brahmanas is white, of kshatriyas red, of vaishyas yellow, and of shudras black."
[Bharadvaja said:] "If the classes of the four orders are divided by colour, then the mixing of colours is seen in all classes.
Desire, anger, fear, greed, grief, worry, hunger and toil arise in all of us; why is class divided?
Sweat, urine, excrement, phlegm, bile and blood flow from the body of all; why is class divided?
The kinds of moving and unmoving beings are countless; of those of many colours, how is the determination of class made?"
[Bhrigu said:] "Those who love violence and falsehood, are greedy, live by all kinds of work, black, fallen from purity: those twice-born became shudras.
Separated by these deeds, the twice-born went to another class; their dharma and sacrificial action are not forbidden to them always.
These are the four classes for whom the Brahmic Sarasvati was formerly ordained by Brahma; through greed they have fallen into ignorance.
Brahmanas who stand in the system of dharma do not lose their austerity, as they ever bear Brahman, vows and rules.
This Brahman was created in the beginning; those who do not know it, ignorant of that, have in this and that place many other kinds of birth.
Pishachas, rakshasas, ghosts, and the many barbarian kinds, whose knowledge and discernment are lost, who act as they please.
The subjects with brahmana rites, resolved on their own dharma, are created by the sages by their austerity, and others by others.
Born of the primal god, with Brahman as root, imperishable and undecaying, that creation called mental is devoted to the system of dharma."
[Bhrigu said:] "He who is purified by the rites beginning with birth-rites, pure, endowed with Vedic study, and established in good deeds,
steady in purity and conduct, eating the remains of offerings, dear to his teacher, ever keeping vows, devoted to truth: he is called a brahmana.
Where truth, giving, self-control, absence of malice, gentleness, forbearance, shame and austerity are seen, he is held to be a brahmana.
He who follows the work of the kshatriya, is esteemed for Vedic study, and delights in giving and taking is called a kshatriya.
He who, pure, engages ceaselessly in agriculture, cow-keeping and trade, endowed with Vedic study, is called a vaishya.
He who ever delights in eating anything, does every kind of work, is impure, has abandoned the Veda and good conduct, is held to be a shudra.
If this mark is found in a shudra and is not found in a twice-born, the shudra is not a shudra and the brahmana is not a brahmana.
By every means, the restraint of greed and anger is to be known as the purifier, and so too self-restraint.
One should ever guard austerity from anger, fortune from envy, learning from honour and dishonour, and the self from heedlessness.
He whose undertakings are all without desire for results and bound only by renunciation, whose every oblation is in renunciation, is the renouncer and the wise.
Harming no being, one should walk the way of Maitrayana; one should not go where there is distrust, and in trust one should hold the mind.
Having given up possessions, one should be a master of the senses by intelligence; one should resort to a state free of grief, fearless here and hereafter.
One who ever practises austerity, is self-controlled, a sage with restrained self, wishing to conquer the unconquered, should be unattached amid attachments.
What is grasped by the senses is called manifest; what is to be known as unmanifest is grasped by inference and is beyond the senses.
One should restrain the mind in prana, and set prana in Brahman; from extinction alone is extinction, and one should think of nothing; the brahmana is happiness, Brahman; by that he reaches it.
Ever joined with purity, endowed with right conduct, and compassionate toward beings: that is the mark of the twice-born."
[Bhrigu said:] "Falsehood is the form of darkness; by darkness one is led downward; those seized by darkness do not see the light covered by darkness.
Heaven is called light and hell darkness; both are gained by those who move on earth through truth and falsehood.
There, such is the livelihood in the world, mixed of truth and falsehood: dharma and adharma, light and darkness, sorrow and happiness.
There what is truth is dharma; what is dharma is light; what is light is happiness. And what is falsehood is adharma; what is adharma is darkness; what is darkness is sorrow.
Here it is said: the discerning, looking upon the creation of the world through bodily and mental pains and pleasures and the rise of unhappiness, are not bewildered.
There the discerning should strive for release from sorrow; for happiness of beings is impermanent here and hereafter.
As the moonlight does not shine on the moon seized by Rahu, so happiness falls away from beings overcome by darkness.

That happiness is said to be of two kinds, bodily and mental. In this world and the next, all undertakings are said to be for the sake of happiness; there is nothing more excellent than the fruit of the three aims. This is the desirable special quality; the undertaking of dharma and wealth has this as its cause, and its origin has happiness as its purpose.
In heaven the wind is very pleasant and the fragrance sweet; there is no hunger, thirst, fatigue, old age or sin.
In heaven there is always happiness; here there is both happiness and sorrow; in hell they say there is only sorrow; but the supreme state is equal.
The earth is the mother of all beings; woman is the mother; the man is Prajapati; they know his seed as made of energy.
Thus the making of the world was ordained by Brahma in the beginning; the creatures turn about, each covered by his own deeds."
[Bhrigu said:] "Sin is quieted by oblation, supreme peace is in study, enjoyment comes from giving, and by austerity one gains everything.
They say giving is of two kinds, for the next world and for this; what is given to the good stands by one in the next.
What is given to the bad is enjoyed here; as the gift is given, such is the fruit gained."
[Bharadvaja said:] "What is the practice of dharma of each, or what is the mark of dharma? How many kinds of dharma are there? You should tell me."
[Bhrigu said:] "Those wise ones who are engaged in the practice of their own dharma gain the fruit of dharma; whoever acts otherwise is bewildered."
[Bharadvaja said:] "This fourfold order of stages of life, ordained long ago by the Brahmarshis: of each, their own observances, you should tell me here."

Bhrigu said: "Long ago the blessed one, acting for the good of the world, ordained four stages for the protection of dharma. Among these, they cite residence in the teacher's house as the first stage. Here, trained rightly in purity, rites, discipline and rules, with humble self, he should attend at both twilights on the sun and fire as deities, abandoning drowsiness and sloth, his inner self purified by saluting the teacher, studying the Veda and hearing; bathing at the three pressings, ever tending the celibate's fire and serving the teacher, with his inner self given over to begging alms and the rest, not opposing the teacher's word and instruction, he should be devoted to study gained by the teacher's grace."
Here is a verse: the twice-born who, having propitiated his teacher, gains the Veda attains the fruit of heaven, and his mind is fulfilled.

They call the householder's life the second stage; we shall explain all its marks of conduct. For those who have returned home, with wives, seeking the fruit of practising dharma together, the householder's stage is ordained; for in it the three aims, dharma, wealth and desire, are accomplished. Taking up wealth by blameless work, gained by excellence in study, made by the Brahmarshis, or got by the essence of disputation, or gained through the practice of offerings and the grace of the gods, the householder should carry on the householder's life. They say it is the root of all stages; those who live in the teacher's house, wandering mendicants, and others who practise the dharma of chosen vows and rules, from this very stage have their alms and shares of offerings.

For forest-dwellers, the provision of goods is chiefly from it; these good ones, who see the good way, devoted to study, wander the earth for the sake of visiting holy places and seeing countries; for them are rising to greet, saluting, freedom from envy, speaking kindly, a pleasant face, offering seat, bed and food according to ability, and honouring.
Here is a verse: the guest who goes back disappointed from a man's house gives him his sin and goes away taking his merit.
And here the gods are pleased by sacrificial rites, the ancestors by the funeral offering, the sages by Vedic study, hearing and retaining, and Prajapati by begetting offspring.
There are two verses here: speak affectionately to all beings, words pleasing to the ear; slander and injury, and harshness, are condemned here.
Contempt, ego and hypocrisy are condemned; non-violence, truth and freedom from anger are the austerity belonging to all stages.

And here: garlands, ornaments, clothes, unguents, perfumes, enjoyment, dance, song, music pleasing to the ear, sights lovely to the eye, the enjoyment of many kinds of food, drink, lickables, suckables and things to be eaten, contentment in delighting with one's own wife, and the gaining of the pleasure of desire.
He whose life in the householder's stage is always accomplished in the virtues of the three aims, having enjoyed pleasures here, gains the end of the good.
The householder who lives by gleaning, devoted to the practice of his own dharma, and has given up the undertaking of pleasures of desire, finds heaven not hard to reach.

He who would follow this fixed conduct ordained by the Brahmarshis would burn his faults like fire, and conquer even worlds hard to conquer.
mahabharata:12:185.3	Now the conduct of wandering mendicants is this: releasing themselves from the fire, wealth, wife, household and attachments, shaking off the bonds of affection for themselves, they wander, clod, stone and gold alike, with minds unattached to the undertakings of the three aims, equal toward enemies, friends and neutrals, harming no beings, moving or unmoving, womb-born, egg-born, sweat-born or sprout-born, by word, mind or deed, homeless, resorting to mountains, riverbanks, tree roots and temples; for dwelling they would approach a town or village, five nights in a town and one night in a village, and entering to sustain life only, they would approach the houses of twice-born whose actions are unmixed, with alms taken in a bowl, unasked, turned back from desire, anger, pride, delusion, greed, meanness, hypocrisy, slander, conceit and violence.
Here is a verse: the sage who goes about having given fearlessness to all beings never has fear arise from any being.
He who, having made the fire-offering in his own body, offers the bodily fire in his own mouth with oblations obtained by begging rounds, passes beyond the worlds by the fire of the funeral pyre.
The pure twice-born who practises the stage of liberation as prescribed, joined with a well-resolved mind, calm like fire without fuel, goes to the world of Brahma.
[Bharadvaja said:] "It is heard that there is a world beyond this world, but it is not perceived; I wish to know it; you should tell me."
[Bhrigu said:] "On the northern side of the Himalaya, holy and endowed with all virtues, holy, safe and desirable, that excellent world is spoken of.
There men are without evil deeds, pure, perfectly spotless, free of greed and delusion, and without trouble.
There the fruit of what was done is plainly obtained: some with beds, vehicles and seats, with palaces and dwellings, surrounded by all desires, some shining with gold ornaments.
To some only the sustaining of life falls; some sustain life with great toil.
Here some are devoted to dharma, some are deceitful; some are happy and some unhappy; some poor and some rich.
Here toil, fear, delusion and sharp hunger arise, and greed for wealth in men, by which even the learned are bewildered.
Here are many kinds of worries about the deeds of dharma and adharma; the wise one who knows both is not stained by sin.
Fraud, deceit, theft, slander, envy, injury to others, violence, backbiting and falsehood:
whoever indulges these loses his austerity; but the learned who does not practise them has his austerity grow.
This world is the land of action; having done good and bad here, one gains good by good deeds, and by bad deeds the opposite.
Here formerly Prajapati, the gods and the hosts of sages, having sacrificed, purified by their offerings and austerities, resorted to the world of Brahma.
The northern part of the earth is most holy and auspicious; those born there are people who have done meritorious deeds.
Others doing evil deeds are in animal wombs, and others of spent life perish on the surface of the earth.
Those attached to devouring one another, joined with greed and delusion, turn about here only; they do not go to the northern quarter.
Those who serve their teachers, restrained celibate students, the wise know the path of all the worlds.
Thus this dharma, made by Brahma, has been told by me in brief; he who knows the dharma and adharma of the world is wise."
[Bhishma said:] "Thus addressed by Bhrigu, king, the mighty Bharadvaja, supremely righteous, was astonished and honoured Bhrigu.
This origin of the world has been told to you, king, in full, greatly wise one; what more do you wish to hear?"
[Bhishma said:] "The ill-conducted, of bad behaviour, ill-judging, fond of rashness are famed as the bad; the good have good conduct as their mark.
Men who do not void excrement or urine on the highway, among cattle, or in grain, are fortunate.
Having done the necessary purification and the offering to the gods, they call it men's dharma; having rinsed, he should cross a river.
He should always attend upon the sun, not sleep at sunrise, and mutter the twilight prayer at dusk and dawn, standing at the first and the last.
He should eat with five limbs wet, facing east, in silence; he should not blame food, and should eat both the tasty and the tasteless.
One should not rise with wet hands nor sleep at night with wet feet; this mark of conduct was spoken by the divine sage Narada.
He should always circumambulate a clean place, a willing ox, a cow-pen, a crossroads, and a righteous brahmana.
A common meal for all guests, servants, and one's own people, with the attendants, is praised for a man.
The leavings of a brahmana are nectar, made in the heart by the mother; people attend to truth, and the good attend to truth.
Meat consecrated with the Yajus, from which one has turned back, I do not eat; one should not eat meat in vain, and should avoid the meat of the back.
In his own country or another, he should not let a guest go hungry; having gained the desired fruit of action, he should present it to his elders.
A seat should be given to elders and salutation made; honouring elders, one is joined with life, fame and fortune.
One should not look at the rising sun, nor at a naked woman of another; union should be at the right time, righteous, and private.
The heart of holy places is the holy place; the heart of the pure is pure; all that is done by the noble is purity, as is the touching of hair.
At each meeting he should always ask after comfort, and at dusk and dawn salutation is enjoined for brahmanas.
In a cow-pen, among cows, in the rites of brahmanas, on the road, in study and at meals, one should raise the right hand.
Of trades, the fine trade; of farmers, farming; abundant yield for crops; for the driver, driving; so for cows.
At a meal one should always say "Well provided," at drink "Satisfying," of milk-pudding "Well cooked," and so of gruel and rice with sesame.
At shaving, on a sneeze, at a bath, at a meal, and to all sick people, one should say wishes for long life.
One should not urinate facing the sun, nor look at one's own excrement; one should avoid lying with a wife in the presence of a son, and eating with her.
One should avoid saying "you" and the name of elders; with juniors and equals both are not a fault.
The heart of the sinful declares their sin by its distortion; they perish knowingly, hiding it from the great.
The little-learned hide sin done knowingly; men do not see him, but the dwellers of the three heavens do.
Sin done by a sinner follows sin; dharma done by a righteous man follows the doer.
The fool does not remember sin done here; it comes to the doer as he turns round; as dust comes to the moon, so sin and deed come to the unwise.
Wealth gathered by hope that is not enjoyed in time here the wise do not praise; for death does not wait.
The wise call dharma mental in all beings; therefore one should do good to all beings by mind.
One should practise dharma alone; in dharma there is no helper; what will a helper do for one who has simply reached the rite?
The gods are the source of men, and in heaven the gods have nectar; after death one enjoys happiness from dharma, ever, by them."
[Bhishma said:] "What you ask me, Partha, as 'the self,' I shall explain to you, dear, a happiness yielding the highest good.
Knowing it, a man finds joy and happiness in the world; the gain of its fruit is immediate, and it is for the good of all beings.
Earth, wind, space, water and, fifth, fire: the great elements are the origin and dissolution of all beings.
Then, created there, those great elements go again and again into beings, as the waves of the sea.
As a tortoise, having extended its limbs, draws them in again, so the self of beings, having created beings, draws them in again.
The maker of beings made the five great elements in all beings; and in them he made difference, which the soul observes.
Sound, hearing, and the cavities: these three are born of space; of wind, skin, touch and movement and speech: this is the fourfold.
Form, the eye, and digestion: this is said to be the threefold fire; taste, moisture and tongue are held to be the three qualities of water.
The smellable, the nose and the body are the three qualities of earth; the five elements are the five, and the mind is said to rest in them.
The senses and the mind are its kinds of knowledge, Bharata; intellect is called the seventh, and the knower of the field is again the eighth.
The eye is for seeing; the mind makes doubt; intellect is for determination; the knower of the field stands as witness.
That which sees upward from the soles of the feet, what is below and above: by this know that all this is pervaded within.
In the man the senses are to be known entire; know tamas, rajas and sattva, and the states that rest on them.
Knowing this by intellect, a man, considering the coming and going of beings slowly, gains the highest peace.
Intellect leads the qualities; intellect also leads the senses, with the mind as sixth; without intellect, where are the qualities?
So all this, moving and unmoving, is made of that; it dissolves and arises again; therefore it is so taught.
That by which one sees is the eye; that by which one hears is called the ear; that by which one smells is the nose, and by the tongue one knows taste.
By skin one touches touches; intellect is altered again and again; that by which one conceives some object is mind.
The seats of intellect are fivefold, for separate objects; the five senses they speak of are governed by the unseen one.
Intellect, governed by the Person, abides in three states; sometimes it finds joy, sometimes it grieves.
It does not exist at any time by happiness or by sorrow; so, in the minds of men, it stands in three states.
This intellect, of the nature of states, does not go beyond these three states, like the lord of rivers, the ocean, which does not pass its great shore though full of waves.
Intellect that has gone beyond states acts in the state of mind; rajas, in motion, follows that state.
It always shows all the senses; joy, sattva, rajas, grief, tamas and delusion are the three.
Whatever states there are in this world, all are within these three; thus the whole course of intellect has been explained to you, Bharata.
The wise man should conquer all the senses; sattva, rajas and tamas ever dwell in living beings.
Threefold feeling is seen in all beings: sattvic, rajasic and tamasic, Bharata.
Pleasant touch is the quality of sattva, painful touch the quality of rajas; joined with the quality of tamas, the two are of practical use.
There, what is joined with joy in body or mind, one should then regard as the sattvic state.
And what is joined with sorrow and brings no satisfaction to the self, that is rajas; one should think of it without agitation.
And what is joined with delusion, as if unmanifest, beyond reasoning and unknowable, one should take as tamas.
Joy, delight, bliss, happiness and tranquillity of mind occurring somehow: these are sattvic qualities.
Discontent, torment, grief, greed and impatience are the marks of rajas, seen with and without cause.
Conceit, delusion, heedlessness, sleep and drowsiness, occurring somehow: these are the various tamasic qualities.
He whose mind, far-going, going in many ways, prayerful and doubting, is well restrained, is happy here and hereafter.
See the subtle difference between sattva and the knower of the field: one creates qualities, the other does not create qualities.
As a gnat and a fig-tree are always joined, and as two distinct things are united, so is the union of the two.
By nature they are distinct, yet always joined, as fish and water are joined, so are these two.
The qualities do not know the self; he knows the qualities entirely; looking on the qualities, he thinks himself ever loosened.
By the senses, with intellect as seventh, though motionless and ignorant, he makes a lamp's purpose; the supreme self is like a lamp.
Sattva creates the qualities; the knower of the field watches; this union of sattva and the knower of the field is fixed.
There is no support for sattva or for the knower of the field at all; sattva creates the mind but never the qualities.
When he rightly restrains their rays by the mind, then the self shines out, like a lamp burning in a pot.
The sage who, giving up natural action, is ever delighted in the self, becoming the self of all beings, would go to the highest goal.
As a water-bird, though touched, is not stained, so the one of trained wisdom moves among beings."
Named Madirashva, a lord of the earth on earth, he was always devoted to the science of the bow and to the Veda.
[Vaishampayana said:] "The asuras and the gods were the numerous offspring of Prajapati Daksha, dear, and they competed with each other.
Alas, I have been deceived, a fool, by you of hidden mind, since you first made me trust you, and now you meet this sorrow.
Whoever of them, enraged, seized an eraka reed, king, it then appeared as a thunderbolt, lord.
Therefore imperishable worlds are yours, with your own body; you have reached, best of the Bharatas, the unsurpassed divine goal.
All the perfected ones and the great sages assembled there, where the king of great splendour, the son of Dharma, stood.
